# Diagnosing a No-Start Condition on a 2005 Malibu Ecotec

A 2005 Chevrolet Malibu Classic equipped with the 2.2L Ecotec engine presenting a no-start condition where the motor cranks but fails to ignite is a classic example of a misfire that lacks sufficient energy capture. The symptoms you described—weak pops during cranking and fouled plugs—are telling, but replacing the spark plugs alone often yields diminishing returns if the ignition source itself is compromised.

The fact that the new plugs are producing a weak spark rather than a bright blue arc indicates an upstream issue with the High Voltage (HV) distribution system or the coil pack assembly. On GM vehicles of this era, particularly those without individual coils per cylinder, the ignition module and resistor pack are often integrated into a single unit mounted atop the engine. This design simplifies wiring harness routing but complicates diagnostics because you cannot isolate a single cylinder's failure easily; if one plug fails to fire brightly, it could be a bad plug wire boot (the rubber connector), a failing internal coil leg, or insufficient primary voltage reaching the module.

To verify if the unit is delivering proper voltage without disassembling the entire assembly immediately, you need to measure secondary spark intensity at each cylinder individually. Since there are no separate plug wires, you must inspect the rubber boots attached directly to the HV terminals on the ignition coil pack. Disconnect one boot at a time and hold it against the engine block while cranking the motor. Observe the arc length and color inside the rubber insulation. A healthy system should produce a strong, bright blue arc spanning several millimeters between the center electrode of the plug (if removed) or the gap within the boot itself. If the arc is faint orange or barely visible, the coil pack or its internal resistor circuitry is degrading. This is a common wear item on these engines after 120,000 miles, often exacerbated by heat cycling and oil contamination.

Regarding your suspicion of the crank sensor: while it is plausible that a failing crank position sensor prevents synchronization between the fuel injector pulse width and spark timing, modern ECU logic typically sets a diagnostic trouble code (DTC) before allowing the engine to run poorly or not at all. The absence of stored codes and the fact that the Malibu does not throw any MIL codes while cranking suggests the ECU is receiving valid crank signals but perhaps detecting a cylinder misfire that it hasn't logged yet due to the intermittent nature of the weak spark. However, do not rule out fuel delivery issues entirely just because pressure exists.

You mentioned that fuel squirts when the port is pressed with a screwdriver. While this confirms the pump operates, it does not guarantee optimal injector spray pattern or volume during cranking. The 2005 Malibu uses returnless fuel injection systems where rail pressure needs to be precise for cold starts. If the fuel pressure drops too quickly once the key is turned off and on again, or if the injectors are clogged with varnish from old fuel, you will see weak combustion that mimics an ignition failure.

When troubleshooting the resistor pack and rubber boots, exercise caution regarding static electricity. The HV wires can retain charge even when disconnected. Always ground yourself before handling components to prevent damage to the ECU or injury. If testing reveals low voltage at the coil output but good battery voltage at the primary side of the ignition module, you will likely need to replace the entire ignition assembly. These units are generally non-serviceable as a whole; swapping individual coils is not an option on this architecture.

If the spark tests out strong and fuel pressure holds steady, your focus should shift to verifying the camshaft position sensor signal relative to the crank. A correlation error between these two sensors can cause the ECU to cut spark or fuel during specific RPM ranges, leading exactly to the "weak pop" scenario you are experiencing. Use a multimeter set to AC voltage mode at the TCI connector (if accessible) or a scope if available to compare the amplitude of the signals against manufacturer specifications.
